kp.k: Cuban predicts simulators will compensate for reduced workplace learning
kp.d: In the article dated 24 July 2026, Cuban predicts that workers will have fewer workplace interactions through which to acquire experience and judgment, making AI job simulators an important future training application. His forecast identifies open-source or open-weight technology as a driver but supplies no adoption timetable or evidence of training effectiveness.
qs: The next great AI application, driven by open source, or open weights, will be a job simulator.
How employees gain experience in a future AI world is going to be far different from today
Employees won't have as many touch points in the company to gain knowledge and experience from.

kp.k: Domain experts would build scenario-based training and reshape onboarding
kp.d: Cuban predicts that future workers will train through simulations analogous to those used by pilots and race car drivers. He recommends drawing on knowledgeable employees and stakeholders to create workplace scenarios, presenting this as a substantial change to onboarding. The article describes established simulator use in aviation and racing as the analogy, not evidence that AI workplace simulators already deliver equivalent results.

kp.k: Legal and medical simulations are illustrative possibilities, not findings
kp.d: Mohamed illustrates the prediction with newly qualified lawyers rehearsing depositions, hearings and settlement negotiations, alongside trainee doctors interacting with AI patients and participating in virtual procedures and emergencies. These are hypothetical applications rather than reported deployments. The suggested realism depends on incorporating experienced colleagues' knowledge from law firms and hospitals.
qs: It's easy to imagine a newly qualified lawyer sitting through simulations of depositions, court hearings, and settlement negotiations so they know what to expect.
Or a trainee doctor preparing for real-life situations by speaking with AI patients, assisting in a virtual surgery, and participating in simulated emergencies.
a job simulator could provide practical, realistic training.

kp.k: Roulet frames AI simulation as an extension of existing training
kp.d: Cambridge professor Thomas Roulet qualifies the novelty claim by noting that organizations and business schools already use virtual reality for training, including unconscious bias. He expects such approaches to become more common and argues that AI can generate learning scenarios. Using plumbers and electricians as examples, he associates jobs resistant to AI replacement with coordination, combined skills and rapid contextual analysis.
qs: I don't see this as fundamentally new, but it is probably true that it will become even more common
Jobs that cannot be replaced by AI require coordination, combining skills, fast analysis in space and in context
AI can definitely help generate scenarios that support learning.

kp.k: Cuban favors human collaboration over AI-only performance
kp.d: The article reports Cuban's view that AI remains limited in emotional intelligence and interpreting interpersonal situations. His broader argument favors combining AI productivity with human real-time capacity and judgment; the claimed superior return is his assertion, not a measured finding presented in the article.

pts.k: Cuban predicts AI job simulators will change how workers acquire experience; Mohamed illustrates a possible application to newly qualified lawyers.
pts.d: Mark Cuban predicts that AI job simulators, driven by open-source or open-weights models, will train workers for workplace situations as opportunities to learn through company interactions decline. Theron Mohamed, the article's author, supplies the legal example: newly qualified lawyers could practise depositions, hearings and settlement negotiations in simulations. This is an illustrative possibility, not a reported implementation. Mohamed also envisages simulated training for doctors. Interviewed Cambridge professor Thomas Roulet regards simulation-based training as an extension of existing practice rather than a fundamentally new development and says AI can generate learning scenarios. Cuban additionally advocates combining AI productivity with human judgment rather than relying on AI alone.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The article offers expert commentary and analogies to existing simulator and virtual-reality training, not measured results for AI job simulators.
pts.d: Cuban's claims are forecasts made in X posts. The article contextualises them with established simulator use by pilots and race car drivers. Roulet supplies an expert observation that organisations and business schools already use virtual reality for training, including unconscious-bias training. Mohamed's legal and medical examples are hypothetical. No dataset, benchmark, trial or measured training outcome is presented for AI job simulators or their use in law firms.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The predictions concern an unspecified future and depend on domain-informed scenarios and continued human contributions.
pts.d: The article reports Cuban's forecast in July 2026 but specifies no adoption deadline. His prediction assumes that workers in an AI-shaped workplace will have fewer interpersonal opportunities to acquire experience. He envisages knowledgeable employees and stakeholders creating scenarios; Mohamed makes realistic legal and medical training conditional on drawing on colleagues' knowledge and experience. Roulet qualifies the novelty claim by pointing to existing training practices and forecasts greater prevalence. Cuban's collaboration claim is qualified by AI's reported limitations in reading social situations and exercising emotional intelligence.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Workers and employers are the main affected groups, with newly qualified lawyers and trainee doctors offered as examples.
pts.d: Workers would acquire practical experience through simulated situations rather than depending as heavily on workplace interactions. Employers would change training and onboarding, while experienced employees and stakeholders would contribute domain knowledge to scenario creation. Mohamed envisages newly qualified lawyers becoming familiar with depositions, hearings and negotiations, and trainee doctors practising patient interactions, surgery and emergencies. Roulet names plumbers and electricians as examples of work requiring coordination, combined skills and rapid contextual analysis, for which AI-generated scenarios could support learning. The article does not predict changes to legal fees, law-firm staffing ratios or access to justice.
